title: GCL Season 4 preview: What to expect as the world’s top players head to Bengaluru
summary: The FIDE Tech Mahindra Global Chess League is returning for its fourth season. With its unique format and competition concept, GCL is looking less like an annual chess tournament and more like a mature global sports league. After Dubai, London and Mumbai, Season 4 will take place in the southern Indian city of Bengaluru, from 5th to 13th September. With India being one of the fastest-growing chess markets and following an unprecedented response to Season 3 in Mumbai, hosting the event in the country for the second time in a row builds on strong Indian momentum in world chess. This is where the “India exports not only chess talent but also a chess format” narrative belongs. Season 4 will see Magnus Carlsen’s return to the competition. World Cup winner and India’s rising woman chess star Divya Deshmukh joins the GCL for the first time, while Viswanathan Anand moves from Ganges Grandmasters, where he spent the first three seasons, to PBG Alaskan Knights. The unusually strong generational pairings, the Road2GCL event prior to the season, a more ambitious technology/fan layer, and growing outside investment in franchises point to an exciting new GCL Season ahead. “We are very excited about Season 4 which is designed to deliver a bigger, bolder version of everything done in the previous three events. We will have a significantly larger fan-facing setup than in previous events, a more prominent technology layer with AR/VR and Physical AI, and we already have a refreshed set of teams promising exciting matchups and outcomes,” says Peeyush Dubey, Chairperson, Tech Mahindra Global Chess League. Bengaluru: Chess meets India’s technology capital Season 4 takes place in Bengaluru, marking a clear connection between chess and technology, which has been one of the staple points of GCL since inception. Dubbed “the Silicon Valley of India,” the city is home to India’s best-known tech companies, with a large population of students and tech professionals. This goes hand in hand with GCL positioning technology as a key tool in improving the spectator experience and engagement with chess. Bangalore Palace – the 19th century royal palace built for the Maharaja of Mysore – will host the opening ceremony while the competition itself will take place at The Lalit Ashok luxury hotel. Taking chess beyond the venue, GCL also continued with its Road2GCL programme which was launched in 2025 and saw online and in-person competitions. The year-round engagement platform is designed to bring players, creators, fans to celebrate chess through different events. When GCL launched four years ago featuring a franchise league structure, some doubted the chances of this approach succeeding in chess. Still, with Season 4 lined up, the league has moved from proving that franchise chess can work to building continuity. According to the analysis provided by GCL, the media reach grew 65% from Season 1 to Season 3, while the media value of the project increased 2.4 times. Magnus Carlsen’s return and Divya Deshmukh’s debut From a purely chess perspective, the biggest news of Season Four is the return of Magnus Carlsen after he skipped Season 3. The Norwegian returns as the Icon player of the Alpine APL Pipers, the defending champions of the League. It is not just Carlsen who makes Pipers the top favourites this season. The team lineup features Anish Giri and Vidit Gujrathi on Men’s Superstar boards. The Pipers also strengthened their women’s ranks, with Koneru Humpy being joined by Divya Deshmukh, the rising sensation who took the Women’s World Cup by surprise. At 19, she defeated Humpy in the FIDE Women’s World Cup final in Batumi. The victory made her the first Indian winner of the Women’s World Cup and earnt her the Grandmaster title. The Humpy – Divya tandem also tells another compelling story of GCL: two generations of elite Indian women players in the same team, highlighting that generational dynamics are also a big GCL feature. The team’s Prodigy board will be manned by Volodar Murzin, the 2024 World Rapid Chess Champion. Viswanathan Anand changes teams for Season 4 One of the most visible changes this season involves Viswanathan Anand. After representing Ganges Grandmasters for the first three editions, the five-time World Champion moves to PBG Alaskan Knights and takes their Icon board. Anand will be leading one of the youngest teams in the League: with the 15-year-old Turkish star Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus joining Arjun Erigaisi on the Superstar Men boards. Kateryna Lagno and Nino Batsiashvili fill the Superstar Women positions, while Abhimanyu Mishra (17) makes his league debut as the team’s Prodigy. Anand, therefore, enters Season 4 alongside some of the youngest players in elite chess. The other franchises have taken different approaches. Two-time champions Triveni Continental Kings have retained much of their established core, including Alireza Firouzja, Wei Yi, Alexandra Kosteniuk, and Zhu Jiner. Ganges Grandmasters have built around experience, with Ian Nepomniachtchi taking the Icon board alongside Levon Aronian and Leinier Dominguez. Mumba Masters continue with Maxime Vachier-Lagrave as their Icon, while FYERS American Gambits enter the season with World Champion Candidate Javokhir Sindarov leading a squad that also includes Daniil Dubov and Nihal Sarin. A particularly strong “old guard vs. next generation” season The generational divide is another defining characteristic of Season 4. At one end there are seasoned champions Anand, Carlsen, Aronian, Nepomniachtchi, MVL, Humpy, Kosteniuk. At the other end – rising stars: Divya, Erdogmus, Abhimanyu Mishra, Murzin, Pranav Venkatesh, Leon Mendonca, and others. The team structure of the competition means that different generations will not just be playing against or alongside one another, but they will depend on one another for the team result. Why GCL plays differently from a traditional chess tournament The competition format remains GCL’s biggest competitive differentiator. For those new to GCL, this format is the main thing to understand ahead of the event. Six franchises compete in a double round-robin league stage before the knockouts to determine the champion. title: Chess is getting its own home on the internet: FIDE and World Chess apply for the .chess domain extension
summary: The application for the game’s official top-level domain has been submitted to ICANN – the first chance in over a decade to create one. If approved, every federation, club, tournament and titled player will be able to carry a verified domain name ending in .chess.  LAUSANNE / LONDON, September 1, 2026 – The International Chess Federation (FIDE) and World Chess (LSE: CHSS), FIDE’s official commercial partner, announce that an application has been submitted to ICANN, the organisation that governs internet names, for .chess – a new top-level domain (TLD) built for the game. The application was filed in ICANN’s first new-domain window since 2012, through a dedicated subsidiary of World Chess and on behalf of FIDE. The application was submitted as a community one – this status provides it with potential leverage over any competing applications for the same string through ICANN’s Community Priority Evaluation process.  Today, the chess-related domains are scattered across .com, .org and dozens of country-code strings, and nothing marks them as belonging to the game. .chess changes that. Just as .com serves commerce, .chess will serve one game: a dedicated, officially recognised TLD where every name – be it for  a national federation or a neighbourhood club, a super-tournament or a grandmaster’s own page – is verified as genuine part of the chess world. What .chess means for the chess world National federations will receive dedicated .chess domains, allocated in coordination with FIDE – a common, recognisable internet identifier system for organised chess in every country. Clubs, academies, organisers, platforms, media and players will be able to register names that instantly say what they are: a string built for the game, backed by the institution that has governed it since 1924, and operated by World Chess. Under the agreement, FIDE acts as the institutional sponsor of the domain and receives a share of the revenues it generates, together with an allocation of domains within the TLD. World Chess manages the application, funds the project and, if the application is successful, will operate the extension on FIDE’s behalf. The initiative is a part of the broader programme by FIDE to build the sport’s digital infrastructure. First move for the community Registration will open only if and when ICANN approves the application. Ahead of that, an early-access list is open at worldchess.com/domains: members of the list will receive regular project updates, including notices of the upcoming domain registration availability, allowing them to be among the first to secure the names they are interested in. Viswanathan Anand, Interim FIDE President  “Chess deserves its own place on the internet – one where a player, a parent or a sponsor can see at a glance that a domain is genuinely part of the game. .chess will give our federations and our community a shared, trusted home online, and I am glad that FIDE is anchoring it together with World Chess.” Ilya Merenzon, CEO of World Chess “Chess has everything a major sport needs — ratings, titles, a global federation, a billion-strong audience –  everything except its own territory on the internet. .chess is that territory. Approval is not guaranteed, and ICANN’s process is rigorous. But this is infrastructure the game deserves, and together with FIDE we intend to build it – and to hand every federation, club and player a domain that says exactly who they are. FIDE – the international governing body for chess, recognised by the International Olympic Committee, with 200+ national federations – has endorsed the application as institutional sponsor. The Company’s management believes the application is strongly positioned in the Community Priority Evaluation.” For national chess federations Federations will receive further information from FIDE and World Chess about their dedicated domain names as the ICANN process advances. Questions and expressions of interest can be sent to im@worldchess.com – no action is required at this stage. You can find more information and sign up for alerts at worldchess.com/domains.  About World Chess World Chess (LSE: CHSS) is a London-based chess gaming and entertainment company and FIDE’s official commercial partner. World Chess organised the FIDE World Championship Matches in the USA and the UK and revolutionised the sport by signing the biggest media partnerships in chess history. World Chess is the creator and operator of Armageddon, the chess league for prime-time television. For more information, visit worldchess.com. Media contacts World Chess – Ilya Merenzon, Chief Executive Officer: merenzon@worldchess.com FIDE – Press Office: press@fide.com

title: FIDE September 2026 rating list published
summary: The FIDE September 2026 rating list was primarily shaped by the Grand Chess Tour Sinquefield Cup, the GCT Finals, the Cairns Cup, and several open tournaments across Europe. Wesley So triumphantly returned to the Top 5 Open after a nearly four-year hiatus, following his victory in the Sinquefield Cup and a third-place finish in the Grand Chess Tour Finals. Meanwhile, the 2026 GCT winner, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, climbed to 8th position and is now back in the Top 10. Photo: Lennart Ootes On the women’s list, Tan Zhongyi returned to the Top 5 after a seven-month absence following her triumph at the 2026 Cairns Cup. Biggest rating gains in top 100 Open and Women lists Modipalli Deekshitha WCM IND 2454 (+297) Kaliakhmet, Elnaz WIM KAZ 2347 (+43) Toncheva, Nadya FM BUL 2408 (+36) Puranik, Abhimanyu GM IND 2629 (+26) Lee, Alice IM USA 2453 (+23) Salimova, Nurgyul IM BUL 2439 (+23) Muradli, Mahammad GM AZE 2653 (+23) Guichard, Pauline IM FRA 2344 (+20) Tan, Zhongyi GM CHN 2536 (+16) Yu, Jennifer FM USA 2354 (+14) Deekshitha Modipalli (pictured below)  of India became the biggest rating gainer on record (since we began publishing these reports), boosting her Elo by a phenomenal 297 points following her strong performances at the XIV Torneo Internacional Cidade de Pontevedra “Masters” (+175) and the Leca Chess Open 2026 (+122). Photo: Leca Chess Open These extraordinary results catapulted the Indian rising star straight to 23rd position on the women’s list and third place on the women’s junior list. Remarkably, she earned as many as 469 rating points across just four tournaments! Undoubtedly, the Indian teenager is the player to watch in the coming months. Elnaz Kaliakhmet overperformed at the Kanizsa Open – Group A, earning 43 rating points, while Nadya Toncheva added 36 points to her tally for her third-place finish at the 35th Open Chess Tournament of Kavala. Photo: Maria Emelianova Mahammad Muradli (pictured above) and Abhimanyu Puranik shone in the Türkiye Chess Super League and the French Team Championship, where they collected 26 and 23 rating points, respectively. Notably, the Azerbaijani GM reached a career-high 64th position on the list. The runner-up of the Cairns Cup, Alice Lee (pictured below), finished just a half-point behind the champion but has every reason to celebrate: her strong performance in this elite tournament brought her 23 rating points and her first GM norm. Photo: Saint Louis Chess Club / Crystal Fuller Brandon Jacobson made his debut in the Top 100 Open after winning the 50è Open Internacional d’Escacs Vila de Sitges Grup A, a result that earned him 18 points. Pauline Guichard lost in a tiebreak for the title at the French Women’s Championship, but she might have found solace in gaining 20 rating points and returning to the Top 100 Women.  For more information, visit: https://ratings.fide.com/

title: Batumi to host FIDE World Cadet Championships 2026: Registration now open
summary: The clock is ticking for the world’s brightest young chess talents. FIDE and the Georgian Chess Federation are pleased to announce that the 2026 World Cadet Championships will take place in the Black Sea resort of Batumi, Georgia, from November 21 to 29, 2026. Forty-eight of the planet’s best young players, split across six categories (Open and Girls Under-8, Under-10, and Under-12), will compete in a high-stakes round-robin format over 7 rounds. The time control is 90 minutes per player, plus a 30-second increment starting from move one. All 48 participants are invited players with personal rights, entitling them to free full-board accommodation for the duration of the Championship. Player selection for the 2026 World Cadet Championships is as follows:  3 spots – The three winners of the 2026 World Cup U8-U12. 4 spots – One nomination from each continent. Nominations shall be sent by the Continental Presidents’ offices. 1 spot – Nomination from the organizing federation If a participating federation does not register an invited player for any reason, or if a continent does not accept the invitation by the deadline, the spots will become FIDE EVE wildcards. The deadline for registration is October 12, 2026. In addition to the FIDE titles and medals, the top three players in each category will be awarded a cup, medal, diploma, and a brand-new Apple device. Every participant will receive an official certificate to commemorate their journey. National Federations must handle the registration process for participants and accompanying persons and shall be responsible for the expenses of coaches and parents. Incomplete or individual registrations will not be accepted; only official federation forms submitted by October 12 will be considered. For full details, visa information, and the official registration form, please visit: For full details, visa information, and the official registration form, visit:https://wcc2026.fide.comOr contact: wcc@fide.com Invitation, schedule, regulations (PDF)

title: 2026 2nd FIDE Council Meeting, August 23: List of decisions

CM2-2026-06 To approve the Regulations for the FIDE World Championship Match 2026.   CM2-2026/07 To approve the Regulations for the World Cup 2027 CM2-2026/08 To approve the Regulations for the Women’s World Cup 2027. CM2-2026/09 To note the Constitutional Commission’s report. CM2-2026/10 To note the Global Strategy Commission’s report CM2-2026/11 To note the Arbiters’ Commission’s report CM2-2026/12 To approve the recommendations of the Arbiters’ Commission on Seminars, Classification upgrades, Amendments to the lecturer list, FA norms, and titles. CM2-2026/13 To approve the recommendations of the Qualification Commission on titles.    CM2-2026/14 To approve the proposal of the Qualification Commission to introduce a “Deceased” status or indicator to the FIDE profile instead of hiding it.    CM2-2026/15 To approve the proposal of the Qualification Commission and the General Strategy Commission to add to article 1.2.2 of the Title Regulations “Only players registered with Federations contained within the Continent, Region or Zone organising the event shall be eligible to participate in these events.” CM2-2026/16 To approve the recommendations of the Trainers’ Commission on titles and Academies. CM2-2026/17 To approve the recommendations of the Events Commission on titles. CM2-2026/18 To approve the recommendations of the Chess in Education Commission on titles. CM2-2026/19 To approve the recommendations of the Fair Play Commission on titles. CM2-2026/20 To further discuss the proposed draft of the Laws of Chess by a working group led by FIDE Executive Director V. Bologan. CM2-2026/21 To note the Social Commission’s report. CM2-2026/22To note the Commission’s for Women’s Chess report. CM2-2026/23 To note Continental Presidents’ reports.     CM2-2026/24 To formally refer the complaints regarding the ACC Continental elections to the Constitutional Commission, instructing it to provide a formal opinion on whether there are legal grounds under Article 27.3 for non-recognition of the elections; and also to provide a recommendation on any other legally binding actions to be taken by the Council.  CM2-2026/25 To approve that the Asian Chess Federation shall have its continental elections 21-24 December 2026 in Al Ain, United Arab Emirates.   CM2-2026/26 To acknowledge the information regarding the election of the President of the Afghanistan Chess Federation held on 30 July 2026 and to recognize the results of the said election. To terminate, with immediate effect, the mandate of Mr. Adzhmal Mangal as the Special Envoy for Afghan Chess. To instruct the FIDE Secretariat to update the FIDE Directory and all relevant official records accordingly. CM2-2026/27 To take note of the information regarding the current situation of the Maldives Chess Federation. To recognise the Interim Committee as caretaker for the federation. To appoint Mr. Victor Bologan as FIDE authorised observer for the future elections at the Maldives Chess Federation, with immediate effect and until further notice. To authorize Mr. Bologan also to provide necessary advice and assistance on behalf of FIDE to the Interim Committee and the Federation. CM2-2026/28 To take note of the information regarding the current situation and to welcome the recent developments within the Sierra Leone Chess Federation. To officially recognize Dr. Samzu Agbaje as the duly appointed Delegate of the Sierra Leone Chess Federation to the FIDE Congress, with all associated rights, duties, and responsibilities, effective immediately. To terminate, with immediate effect, the mandate, special powers, and functions previously assigned to Mr. Nigel Short in any capacity in relation to the Sierra Leone Chess Federation, acknowledging that his intervention is no longer required. To instruct the FIDE Secretariat to update the FIDE Directory and all relevant official records to reflect Dr. Samzu Agbaje as the official FIDE Delegate for Sierra Leone.     CM2-2026/29 To take note of the application for Affiliated Membership status submitted by the Somaliland Chess Association. To take note of the opinion provided by the African Chess Confederation (ACC) regarding this application. To reject the application of the Somaliland Chess Association for admission as an Affiliated Member of FIDE. CM2-2026/30 To note the information regarding FIDE Awards and request the FIDE Council members to provide their nominees. CM2-2026/31 To approve the Agenda for the FIDE General Assembly and to request the official opinion of the Constitutional Commission regarding the final composition of the items.

title: Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu wins Grand Chess Tour 2026
summary: Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu overcame a six-point deficit on the final day to defeat Fabiano Caruana 15–13 and claim the 2026 Grand Chess Tour title. In the match for third place, Wesley So prevailed over Vincent Keymer after sweeping all four blitz games. The 2026 Grand Chess Tour season culminated at the GCT Finals, held at the Saint Louis Chess Club from August 22–27. The four highest-ranked full-tour players after the regular season – Seed No. 1 Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, Seed No. 2 Wesley So, Seed No. 3 Fabiano Caruana, and Seed No. 4 Vincent Keymer – contested a knockout tournament for the GCT crown. Each match included two Classical games, two Rapid games, and four Blitz games. The total prize fund was $450,000, distributed as follows: $200,000 for first place, $125,000 for second, $75,000 for third, and $50,000 for fourth. Semifinals Praggnanandhaa defeated Vincent Keymer in convincing fashion, winning the point-heavy classical and rapid segments and punching his ticket to the final before the blitz portion. The second semifinal, Fabiano Caruana vs. Wesley So, was a much closer affair. After the two classical games were drawn, Caruana pulled ahead by winning the bonus blitz game. The opponents then split the points in the rapid encounters to settle the matter in blitz. After scoring victories in the first and third games and drawing the second, Caruana advanced to the final. Final and third-place matchCaruana got off to a strong start, defeating Praggnanandhaa in the first classical game with the white pieces. The Indian GM came very close to leveling the match in the return game but did not manage to capitalize on his winning chances and had to settle for a draw. Heading into the final day six points down (3–9), Praggnanandhaa roared back, winning both rapid games to seize an 11–9 lead. Caruana evened the score after winning the second blitz game, but Praggnanandhaa responded strongly in the next one, restoring a two-point lead.  The Indian GM achieved a completely winning position in the final blitz game but opted to force a draw by perpetual check, securing the title. In the third-place match, Vincent Keymer obtained a two-point edge over Wesley So after winning the bonus blitz game (both classical games were drawn). The opponents traded victories in the rapid segment, but the blitz portion of the match was completely dominated by So, who won all four games to secure third place. title: FIDE stands with Nepal’s chess community in the wake of devastating floods
summary: Dear President and Members of the Nepal Chess Federation, On behalf of FIDE and in my capacity as Interim President, I wish to express my deepest condolences and solidarity following the tragic floods that struck Nepal on 26 August. We are deeply saddened by the loss of life and the suffering caused by this devastating disaster. Our thoughts are with all those who have lost loved ones, their homes, or their livelihoods, as well as with the communities affected by the floods.  At this difficult time, I would like to convey FIDE’s sincere support to the Nepal Chess Federation and to the entire chess community in Nepal. We stand with you in solidarity and hope that the rescue and recovery efforts will bring relief to those affected and that the country will recover swiftly from this tragedy. Please convey our heartfelt condolences to all members of the Nepalese chess community and, above all, to those who have been personally affected by this disaster. With deepest sympathy and solidarity, Viswanathan AnandInterim President FIDE

title: Chess enters school curriculum in Kurdistan, Iraq
summary: Chess has officially entered the school curriculum in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, marking an important milestone for chess education and bringing the game’s educational benefits to a new generation. The initiative was developed through the efforts of Khanzad Chess Club, in cooperation with the Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Education and with the support of the Iraqi Chess Federation. By introducing chess into schools, the project aims to use the game not only as a sport but also as an educational tool that encourages critical thinking, concentration, creativity, discipline, patience, and problem-solving. The initiative is the result of cooperation among educational authorities, chess institutions, and chess professionals. Khanzad Chess Club played a pioneering role in developing the project and preparing the educational materials. Under the leadership of its President, Dr. Dlzar Hamasalih Qadir, the club prepared the specialized chess curriculum and educational content for the “Chess for Schools” project, helping transform the idea of introducing chess into schools into a structured educational program for students and teachers. Dr. Dlzar Hamasalih Qadir (Right), President of Khanzad Chess Club, introduces the Chess for Schools textbook to Mr. Masrour Barzani, Prime Minister of the Kurdistan Region. A major step came with the Kurdistan Regional Government Ministry of Education’s decision to include chess in the educational program for students in Grades 7, 8, and 9. As part of the initiative, a dedicated 15-page section on chess was included in the official Physical Education Teacher’s Guide, providing teachers with material to support the program’s implementation. Dr. DlzarHamasalihQadir and FI KardoAko explain the project to Dr. Alan Hama Saeed, Minister of Education of the Kurdistan Regional Government, and Mr. Burhan Argoshi, Senior Advisor to the Minister of Education. Before the project began in schools, attention was given to preparing the teachers who would introduce chess to their students. A one-week training course was organized for 150 Physical Education teachers from Erbil. Hosted by Khanzad Chess Club, the course was conducted by the club’s international trainers in coordination with the Kurdistan Regional Government Ministry of Education. The participating teachers received certificates upon completing the course. Mr. Dhafer Madhloom, President of Asian Zone 3.1 and the Iraqi Chess Federation (right), and Mr. Bijan Saeed, Director of School Activities in Erbil, present certificates to participating teachers following the successful completion of the training course. The Iraqi Chess Federation has also played an important supporting role in the initiative. Its continued encouragement and cooperation have contributed to the development and promotion of chess education and activities in Iraq, supporting the broader effort to make chess more accessible to young people. With the curriculum prepared, teachers trained, and institutional support in place, the “Chess for Schools” project is now being implemented in schools across the Kurdistan Region. Students are being introduced to chess as part of their educational experience, learning the principles of the game while developing intellectual and personal skills that can extend beyond the chessboard. Students participate in the “Chess for Schools” program in the Kurdistan Region. For the students taking part, the project offers more than an introduction to the rules of chess. The game encourages them to analyze situations, consider different possibilities, make thoughtful decisions, and learn the value of patience and responsibility – skills that can be useful both in the classroom and in everyday life. The cooperation among the Kurdistan Regional Government Ministry of Education, Khanzad Chess Club, and the Iraqi Chess Federation provides an example of how chess organizations and educational authorities can work together to bring chess into the classroom. It also creates a foundation for the continued development of chess in schools throughout the Kurdistan Region. Young students take part in the “Chess for Schools” program, representing a new generation of learners and future chess players in the Kurdistan Region. The introduction of chess into the school curriculum is a significant achievement for the Kurdistan Region and an encouraging development for chess education in Iraq. It shows how a long-term educational vision, supported by cooperation between government authorities and chess organizations, can bring the benefits of chess to a wider generation of students. As chessboards find their place in classrooms, they can also open new paths in the minds of young learners. With every move, students learn to think ahead, consider their choices, learn from mistakes, and approach challenges with patience and confidence. In this way, chess can become more than a game taught at school – it can become a lasting source of knowledge, creativity, and inspiration for the next generation.
